Jordan / team — quick notes for the call:

- From a runtime perspective we validate image signatures on pull and at start-of-job. For air-gapped installs the policy is the same; the difference is the distribution path.
- Recommended: detached signatures (cosign or similar), SHA256 checksums, and an attestation bundle per-image that includes build metadata and a timestamp.
- We typically require customers to mirror a small set of images into a local registry (offline registry mirror) and sign the mirror update with a split-signing model (build team signs, security co-signs).
- During canary we drive traffic to the local registry and enforce a strict allowlist of image digests. If a digest mismatch occurs the agent refuses to start.

I'll demo the verification logs on the call and outline the agent failure modes.

-Vivek

Jordan — following up with a concrete, offline-friendly sequence we recommend. This is the technical playbook we will review on the call; please let us know what you already have so we can skip redundant steps.

1) Build and sign:
   - Build images in your secure CI; produce image digest and metadata.
   - Sign with cosign (recommended) or PKCS7 detached signatures. Example: cosign sign --key kms://hsm/airgap-key registry.prod.acme/app:20261130
   - Produce an attestations.tar (signed) containing SBOM, build-id, git commit, and timestamp.

2) Package for transfer:
   - Create a transfer bundle: images.tar (images exported with podman/ctr), attestations.tar, checksums.txt, manifest.json, and a signature file (images.tar.sig).
   - Use incremental naming (images_20261130.tar) and include a manifest with digests.

3) Transport and ingest at site:
   - Transfer via a validated jumpbox under your control (airgap host). Jumpbox must have read-only mounting for the transfer medium and run a verifier agent.
   - On-site operator runs: sha256sum -c checksums.txt; cosign verify --key <pubkey> images.tar.sig; unpack to local registry.
   - Mirror the contained images into the offline registry: podman load -i images_*.tar && podman push --tls-verify=false localhost:5000/app:tag

4) Verification & attestation enforcement:
   - Redwood agents will verify the local registry digest against the allowlist at container start. The allowlist should be generated from manifest.json and stored in /etc/redwood/allowlist.json (managed by ops).
   - Store key material in an on-prem HSM or an air-gapped KMS. If no HSM, use an offline hardware token and a split-signing ceremony.

5) Canary & rollback:
   - Canary: push to dedicated canary namespace, route 5-10% traffic manually, observe metrics for N minutes.
   - Rollback: keep last-3 images in the registry; trigger rollback by updating the allowlist to previous digest and restarting the agent via the local orchestrator. Include a documented manual rollback runbook.

6) Audit & evidence:
   - Keep attestations and transfer logs in a tamper-evident store (signed tar + timestamping). Provide a digest to Redwood for cross-checking during support calls.

Command examples included in the runbook during the call. Main risks to call out: key compromise during transfer, stale manifests, and operator errors copying artifacts. We recommend a pre-transfer checklist and a post-ingest verification step that must pass before scheduling canary traffic.

-Priyom

Adding a couple of operational notes for the record:

- Keep canary windows short and instrumented. For offline sites use local synthetic checks in addition to real traffic sampling.
- Automate allowlist promotion: once the canary window passes the ops runbook should include a single command to promote manifest digests from canary namespace to prod allowlist.
- Retain at least 7 days of image and manifest backups per cluster to simplify rollbacks; older images can be archived to read-only storage.

I'll capture the commands and a minimal emergency rollback checklist in the runbook.
